premise: CARRIED VERBATIM FROM THE SLICE, and unchanged by it. The server owns the data: PostgreSQL is the record and the phone is a cache. The phone reads the whole log — one conditional GET, about 85 KB — before its first frame, exactly as it reads the file today, so `logbookProvider` stays synchronous and no screen grows a loading state. Writes go to the server and wait for it; there are no offline writes and no reconciliation. Photographs live in S3-compatible object storage, uploaded straight to the bucket and read back through short-lived signed URLs, and the log carries an object id and never a URL. When the server is unavailable a write is refused rather than queued. What is not being built: multi-device conflict handling, invites, roles, password reset, email, a rendered share page, server-side preferences, and real photograph capture.

decisions.status: NEW — taken by this plan, and it is first because it is the only irreversible thing in it
decisions.title: The two sample photographs are captured into this repository before anything else happens
decisions.evidence: Measured 23 Aug 2026. On the client's `wipe/mock-data` branch — the branch the human is working on — `assets/imagery/` does not exist and pubspec.yaml declares no assets at all. On `main` the two files are there: card-ireland.png at 529,392 bytes and hero-mountain.png at 555,376 bytes, sha256 8dfb203b… and e66b552e…. All 284 photographs in the fixture point at one or the other, and so do every coverAsset on trips, cities and places.
decisions.reasoning: This is DEC-75's situation again and it has not been noticed. DEC-75 caught the 85 KB fixture in a scratch directory and copied it because once the Dart source was deleted it could never be regenerated. The IMAGERY is the other half of that document and nobody copied it. It exists on one branch of a repository this plan may not write to, and the branch that deleted it is the one being developed on. A `git branch -D main` or a force-push and the fixture points 284 times at bytes nobody has. The alternative — substitute any two PNGs — is worse than it sounds: the object ids are content hashes, so different bytes are different ids, and every measurement in this document that names a digest stops being reproducible.
decisions.consequence: internal/media/testdata/card-ireland.png and internal/media/testdata/hero-mountain.png, byte-identical, with a README beside them recording where they came from and that they are FIXTURE IMAGERY and not anybody's photographs. 1,084,768 bytes of binary in a Go repository, which is a real cost and is the reason this is a decision rather than a chore — see open_rulings[2]. Their digests become named constants that R3's commit route, R4's seed and R8's mint all resolve against, so a substitution is caught by a failing checksum rather than by a wrong picture.

decisions.status: NEW — taken by this plan; the alternative was measured and is worse
decisions.title: The share flag defaults move to the client's, in migration 0002, rather than the upsert naming the columns
decisions.evidence: The schema: three columns `NOT NULL DEFAULT false`. The client: Trip.defaultSharePhotos = true, Trip.defaultShareNotes = true, Trip.defaultShareCoordinates = false, and stopSharing writes exactly those three constants back. The upsert names none of the three, deliberately (SF6), so a create takes the schema's answer and a rename leaves them alone.
decisions.reasoning: Two places could carry the truth and only one of them survives contact with the second writer. If the upsert names the columns on INSERT it must NOT name them on the UPDATE branch, which is an ON CONFLICT clause that sets some columns and not others in a statement whose whole point is that it sets everything — the shape that gets 'tidied' by the next person and silently starts overwriting H1's switches. If the DEFAULT carries it, a create is right with no Go involved, a rename is untouched, and DEC-80's own leg is a SELECT. Moving the DEFAULT also puts the value where the public read and any future writer will find it. It costs a second migration, which this project has never run — and that is a benefit rather than a cost, because the forward-only runner's second-file path is currently exercised only by tests.
decisions.consequence: migrations/0002 alters two DEFAULTs and nothing else. share_coordinates stays false, and the comment says why in the client's own words: a pin on your accommodation is not something to hand out by link, so it has to be actively turned on. EXISTING ROWS ARE NOT REWRITTEN — a DEFAULT change is forward-only by definition, and the only rows in existence are the slice arc's, which the arc destroys on every run. stopSharing (R5) still writes the three values EXPLICITLY rather than relying on the DEFAULT, because it is an UPDATE and a DEFAULT does not reach an UPDATE; the leg asserts all three by name against the client's constants.

decisions.title: `make seed` is `cmd/seed`, a separate binary, and never a flag on `cmd/api`
decisions.evidence: internal/seed's own doc comment already says it: the command 'takes its DSN as an explicit flag rather than from the environment, so that an ambient DATABASE_URL cannot aim it at a real database by accident'. v6's S12 planned `cmd/api/seed.go`.
decisions.reasoning: A flag on the server binary puts a command that writes a whole database inside the artefact that ships to production, where the DSN it would use is the one already in the environment. The refusal — 'the target refuses against a non-empty log rather than merging' — is a guard, and a guard inside a production binary is one review away from being made overridable for a good reason. A second main package costs a directory and a line in the Makefile, and it makes `go list ./cmd/...` the whole answer to 'what can this repository run'.
decisions.consequence: cmd/seed, taking -dsn (required, no default, no environment fallback), -force and -reset. cmd/api's existing import sweep — which asserts pgx is imported exactly once, blank, in main — gains a sibling assertion that cmd/api imports nothing from internal/seed. `-sweep-media` (DEC-38) is NOT covered by this decision and stays a flag on cmd/api when it lands: a sweep is an operational command run against the database it is deployed beside, which is the opposite argument.

decisions.status: NEW — taken by this plan, and it is the ordering decision the eight steps hang on
decisions.title: Object storage and the media routes come BEFORE the seed, and the seed writes bytes as well as rows
decisions.evidence: photos.asset is NOT NULL with a CHECK of `^[0-9a-f]{64}$` and a foreign key to media_objects(traveller_id, id). The fixture's asset values are `assets/imagery/card-ireland.png` and `assets/imagery/hero-mountain.png`. Neither satisfies the CHECK, so the fixture cannot be loaded at all until its assets are object ids and those objects exist as rows.
decisions.reasoning: Three orderings were available. (a) Seed FIRST, inserting media_objects rows with uploaded_at set and no bytes anywhere: cheapest, and it manufactures a row the commit route would never have created — a committed object with nothing behind it — which is a lie in the record and it would be the seed's lie, in the one dataset every later leg is written against. (b) Seed first with uploaded_at NULL: honest, satisfies the FK (which references the primary key, not the upload state), and leaves a seeded log whose every photograph mints a URL to nothing, so R8's public read would be developed against a bucket that is empty. (c) Media first. It is the one v6 already chose, for a reason that still holds — V3-B8: a committed-asset validator with no positive test passes 'an uncommitted asset is refused' perfectly — and it is the only ordering under which R4's whole-log round trip is a statement about the real system.
decisions.consequence: R2 (the store) and R3 (the routes) precede R4 (the seed). R4's seed uploads TWO files through internal/media and commits them through the same code path POST /v1/media/{id}/commit uses, then rewrites the fixture's four asset-bearing columns and loads eleven tables. The cost is that the biggest evidence win in the plan — four lists that have never been read back from PostgreSQL — waits three steps. That is stated rather than hidden, and it is the single thing to challenge if a reviewer thinks the order is wrong.

decisions.title: The asset rewrite is one named function with its own legs, and it REFUSES an unmapped locator
decisions.evidence: The census: two distinct locators across 284 photographs and three coverAsset columns.
decisions.reasoning: The alternative — a second generated fixture (DEC-52, deleted here as OE-8) — makes the transformation invisible, because what you compare against is the output rather than the rule. A named function is a thing a mutation can break: point one locator at the wrong digest and R4's round-trip leg names the field. And the refusal is what a substitution silently gives you instead of an error: a fixture that grows a third image, or a typo'd path, would otherwise be loaded with its asset unchanged and rejected by a CHECK constraint three layers down, with the message naming a regexp rather than a locator.
decisions.consequence: `logbook.RewriteAssets(doc Document, byLocator map[string]string) (Document, error)` in internal/logbook, returning an error naming the unmapped locator. It rewrites FOUR columns — Photo.Asset and the three CoverAssets — because DEC-46 made all four object ids and DEC-58 put a foreign key on all four. Its legs include the negative: a document holding a locator the map does not carry is refused, and the error names it.

decisions.status: NEW — taken by this plan, inheriting the client's scar rather than its data model
decisions.title: Every step that adds a route adds its arc assertion in the SAME COMMIT
decisions.evidence: VS6 shipped two routes green in `go test` and answering 404 in the running container, and recorded it. VS7 shipped two more and the note grew from two routes to four. VS8 closed it — and the defect VS7 actually found (`"cityIds":null`) was found by pointing the binary at a real database, not by any of 71 mutations. Separately, two of the arc's own legs were decoration until VS8 broke them on purpose: `curl -o` does not truncate its output file when a response has no body, so the 304's empty-body assertion measured the PREVIOUS request's 333 bytes and passed.
decisions.reasoning: agent-graph-spec-V4 §6.7's second half asks for the client's hard-won LESSONS and not only its entities. This is this repository's own, learned twice: a green suite cannot tell a guard from a decoration, and neither can a suite that has never been pointed at the real thing. Batching the arc work into a final step recreates the gap for the length of six steps.
decisions.consequence: scripts/slice-arc.sh grows in R3, R5, R6, R7 and R8. Its assertion count is re-derived per step and recorded; it is 76 today. The rule has a corollary the record already paid for: an ABSENCE assertion in shell is the easiest kind to write so that it cannot fail, so every new absence leg removes its output files before the request and counts a file curl never created as zero.

decisions.status: NEW — taken by this plan; DEC-62 is what it applies
decisions.title: The Service layer is written for exactly three operations and for nothing else
decisions.evidence: DEC-62 ruled it and named the three: refilePhoto, removePlace, and the media commit flow. It also ruled, in the same breath, that most of the 24 routes are plain CRUD where a service method forwards to the repository and returns, and that such a file is noise.

A leg asserts the Service has no methods beyond the three, so a fourth arrives as a decision rather than as drift.

deferred_decisions.deferred_to: unscheduled, and this deferral carries an argument for never

notes: ROUTE ARITHMETIC, RE-DERIVED AND NOT DECREMENTED: 23 rows above = 1 healthz + 4 auth/traveller + 1 read + 12 entity-and-share writes + 3 media + 1 public + the PUT trips already live. v6 had 24; this plan deletes GET /v1/me (OE-7) and adds nothing, so 23. FIVE are live at aeac3ed and EIGHTEEN are built here, distributed 3 + 6 + 3 + 5 + 1 across R3, R5, R6, R7, R8. THE COMMAND GOES IN CLAUDE.md, NOT THE NUMBER.

THE ONLY HARD ORDERING IS R2 -> R3 -> R4, and DEC-79 is the argument. Everything after R4 depends on R4 only for its FIXTURE: R5, R6 and R7 write cascades whose legs are worth having against 284 photographs and nearly worthless against one trip. They would compile without it.

steps.size: LARGE, and it is the one step where a defect is a privacy leak rather than a bug
steps.work:
1. GET /l/{token} resolves a LIVE share link — `revoked_at IS NULL`, through the global unique index on token, arriving with no traveller in hand — and answers docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md's allowlist and nothing else. Unauthenticated, rate-limited, and the path is REDACTED from the log, because a live capability in an access log is the capability.
2. THE GUARD IS STRUCTURAL, not a substring search. Parse the emitted document, walk it, and assert the key set AT EVERY LEVEL EQUALS the allowlist. That is what lets a city's centre stay visible: the assertion becomes 'the only `lat` in this document is under cities[].centre', which a grep for 'lat' cannot express and which v1's substring version was both unsatisfiable and blind.
3. IT FILTERS ROWS AS WELL AS KEYS, and the key walk cannot substitute for it: a wishlist place, and a place in the same city belonging to a DIFFERENT trip, must appear in neither. This is v6's V4-B2 and it is the finding that says a key-set assertion feels complete and is not.
4. TWO LEAK SURFACES, not one. The allowlist is the first. The second is that when sharePhotos is false a signed URL must not be MINTED AT ALL — not minted and withheld, not minted and filtered — because a minted URL is a live capability whether or not it is in the response, and because it costs an HMAC nobody asked for.
5. sharePhotos off removes `photos` entirely. shareNotes off strips Visit.note AND Photo.caption — both, because the client's own copy calls them 'in your words'. shareCoordinates off strips Place.coordinates, Photo.coordinates, Photo.accuracyMetres AND Walk.points, because a track is a coordinate sequence; the city CENTRE stays, because it is coarse and it is what a map opens on with no pins.

That is correct for a direct connection and wrong the moment a proxy appears, at which point every request arrives from the proxy's address and the rate limiter is ONE BUCKET FOR THE WHOLE INTERNET — in front of an unauthenticated Argon2 surface costing 64 MiB per attempt and a public share read. It has been deferred twice, by the slice and by this plan, and it is now the largest single thing standing between this stack and anything a second machine can reach. The leg that settles it exists nowhere: two different X-Forwarded-For values behind ONE RemoteAddr, and separate buckets.

DEF-01 and DEF-02: how a physical iPhone reaches the stack, and which hostname the bucket is addressed by.

The `.env.example` / compose / config.Load coverage test — one leg, and the last item on EVIDENCE.md's 'guarded by nothing' list that a single test closes. Delete ARGON2_MAX_CONCURRENT from the compose file today and `make check` stays green while the container refuses to start.
`-sweep-media`: the orphan sweep with its grace window, over four liveness columns rather than one (DEC-46). It has a schedule of nobody.
README, and docs/BEFORE-A-PUBLIC-DEPLOY.md ticked by a human with a device.
next_slice.and_after_that: The large seed generator — internal/seed.Generate, 50,000 photographs across three travellers — and DEC-70's index question at a size where the planner's answer means something. It is also the only thing left that would make DEF-03's timeout numbers measurable.

risks.risk: R2 is the largest single increase in this project's dependency footprint and it lands in one commit. Sixteen new modules against a repository that has had twenty in total, into a package that signs capabilities.
risks.mitigation: Measured before adoption rather than after: minio-go v7.3.0 declares exactly `go 1.25.0`, tidy leaves the directive alone, build and vet exit 0. The command is in base.measured. The shipped set — as opposed to the module graph — is re-derived from the binary with `go version -m bin/api` once R2 lands, because `go list -m all` reports 235 and that number would be quoted wrongly by the next reader.

risks.risk: THE SHARPEST THING IN R2: `PresignedPutObject` and `Presign` both FAIL OPEN. Reach for either and no checksum is signed, the upload succeeds, the commit's HEAD succeeds, and the address space is poisoned by any client that lies. It looks correct through the whole of development because MinIO is a forgiving verifier.
risks.mitigation: A grep that CAN fail, in the definition of done. The checksum leg against a PINNED MinIO tag. And — this is the part that makes it evidence — the INTERMEDIATE RED is recorded: implement with PresignedPutObject first, watch the bucket return 200 for the wrong bytes, then sign the checksum. A leg written after the correct implementation cannot say it would have caught this.

risks.risk: R4's round-trip leg is the strongest leg in the plan and it is also the one most likely to be weakened rather than satisfied. Its first red will be an enormous cmp.Diff across thirty keys, six ORDER BYs and a jsonb unnest, and the tempting response is to narrow it to the fields that pass.
risks.mitigation: Paste the whole first red into EVIDENCE.md before fixing anything. It is the inventory of what had never been tested, and it is worth more as a record than as a to-do list. The per-field legs underneath it — the visits ordering, the date rendering — exist because the round trip cannot say WHICH thing broke, not so that the round trip can be replaced by them.

risks.risk: R6's statement-order defect and R7's unordered-SELECT defect are both the kind that pass a single green run. The refile mutation in particular can return the right row by luck.
risks.mitigation: `-count=10` on the refile legs and the FAILURE RATE recorded rather than a single red — the same discipline DEC-06's snapshot proof already needs, and the DBA's own measurement (1 of 8 unlocked writers succeeding) is the reason it is not paranoia.

risks.risk: THE FORMAT VERSION. Nothing in R1-R8 is blocked by it and everything after R8 is. The server emits 2, the client accepts only 1, exactly, and the client has no HTTP path at all — apiBaseUrlProvider throws by design and logbookProvider.build() is synchronous by decision.
risks.mitigation: open_rulings[1], docs/CLIENT-PREREQUISITES.md as R1's first item, and a statement in CLAUDE.md that GET /v1/logbook's document is currently unreadable by the client it was written for. It is written as a fact rather than as a risk because it is not a probability — it is the present state.

risks.risk: R8 is the one step where a defect is a privacy leak, and its two leak surfaces are of different kinds: an allowlist a key-walk can check, and an HMAC that must not be computed at all.
risks.mitigation: docs/PUBLIC-ENVELOPE.md written in R5 by somebody not holding the handler. The row-filter leg the key walk cannot substitute for. And the mint leg counting HMAC calls through an instrumented store — because an assertion about the response body is structurally unable to see a URL that was minted and dropped.

risks.risk: DEC-31's whole-log read has never been tested at whole-log size. The slice plan said so in terms and forbade the re-plan from treating the slice as evidence for it.
risks.mitigation: R4 is the first step that can measure it, and its acceptance check records the response size and the time. The performance lens is required for exactly this reason and has not run.

risks.risk: Seven of eight required review lenses have not run, and this plan touches a schema, an auth surface, a public endpoint, a new external service and four irreversible user actions.
risks.mitigation: None available inside this document. §6.1a makes it a blocker at `Plan OK?` and §9 asks for two passes minimum on distinct lenses. `database` and `security` first: R2 and R8 should not be started without them, and the last time nobody wore the database hat a blocker survived three passes because a different foreign key deleted the row first.

risks.risk: The client work this plan discovers is substantial and this plan cannot do any of it: a sign-in screen that does not exist, DEC-45's seventh dependency, four sentences of copy, an ImageProvider keyed by object id, an async seam through roughly thirty providers, a format bump, and — new — an app with no bundled imagery at all, because wipe/mock-data deleted assets/imagery/ and pubspec.yaml declares no assets.

risks.risk: `make slice` is run by nobody but a human. There is no CI, `make check` is deliberately fast and Docker-free, and the phases that need a daemon are opt-in — so the arc's evidence is only as fresh as the last time somebody ran it.
risks.mitigation: Unchanged and unmitigated, and said out loud rather than left for a green file to imply otherwise. DEC-81 at least keeps the arc in step with the routes, which is the failure this actually causes.

risks.risk: R1 is trivial in size and irreversible in one direction. If the client's `main` branch is deleted or force-pushed before R1 lands, the two photographs are gone and every digest in this document stops being reproducible.
risks.mitigation: R1 is first, and its `why_first` says that this is the reason rather than sequencing. It is the shortest step in the plan; there is no version of this work in which doing it later is better.

open_rulings.severity: BLOCKER for client integration; blocks nothing in R1-R8
open_rulings.question: The server stamps `"version": 2` and refuses to emit anything else. The client refuses anything but `1`, with exact equality, and quarantines the file. Which side moves?
open_rulings.what_is_already_true: DEC-40 moved the wire to 2 because Photo.asset and the three coverAssets change MEANING — a bundle path before, an object id now — and said it 'costs nothing today because nothing has shipped against this backend'. True of the backend. The client has shipped: it is a working application with a working decoder, it does not implement DEC-53's negotiation, and it has no HTTP path to negotiate over (apiBaseUrlProvider throws by design).
open_rulings.the_options: (a) The client bumps logbookFormatVersion to 2 in the same pass that teaches it to read an object id — which is honest, because `asset`'s meaning genuinely changed and a client that reads a digest as a bundle path draws a failure plate 284 times. (b) The server emits 1 as well as 2, which means two shapes and two emitters for a difference that is not shape but meaning. (c) DEC-53's negotiation gets a client half, which is (a) plus a header.
open_rulings.recommendation: (a). It is one constant and one migration note on the client side, it is scheduled in CLIENT-PREREQUISITES either way, and (b) buys a compatibility nobody can use — the client cannot render an object id at version 1 any more than at version 2.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: It is client work in a read-only repository, and DEC-40 is a ruled decision whose stated justification has turned out to be half true.

open_rulings.severity: blocker for R1, and R1 is first
open_rulings.question: May 1,084,768 bytes of PNG be committed to this Go repository?
open_rulings.what_is_already_true: The two files exist only on the client's `main` branch. `wipe/mock-data` deleted assets/imagery/ and pubspec.yaml declares no assets at all. All 284 photographs in the reference fixture, and the coverAsset on trips, cities and places, point at one of the two. DEC-75 faced exactly this for the 85 KB JSON and captured it, recording that once the Dart source was deleted it could never be regenerated.
open_rulings.recommendation: Capture them. The alternative is not 'no binaries in the repo' — it is that the reference fixture points 284 times at bytes nobody has, and that every digest in this document stops being reproducible. Substituting different PNGs is worse: the object ids are content hashes, so different bytes are different ids.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: Committing binaries to a source repository is a policy question, and this is the first time it arises here.

open_rulings.severity: minor, but it touches an APPROVED artefact
open_rulings.question: `GET /v1/me` is deleted (OE-7) because it has no caller: the only traveller field the client renders is `name` and that arrives inside GET /v1/logbook. Does GATE-L12's clearance survive the deletion of a route the approved sequence diagrams may draw?
open_rulings.recommendation: Ratify the deletion. But say so explicitly rather than letting it be inferred — the whole reason GATE-L12 is recorded with a scope and a hash is that this project once described artefacts as approved that no human had seen.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: An approval with no scope is the same defect wearing a tick, and only the approver can say whether a change is material.

open_rulings.severity: minor, and it is a naming disagreement between two artefacts
open_rulings.question: The database service is `postgres` in the shipped compose file, in DATABASE_URL, and in the slice plan's own text. v6's S22 calls it `db`. CLAUDE.md flags the disagreement and says the re-plan must settle it rather than inherit both.
open_rulings.recommendation: `postgres`. It shipped, DATABASE_URL names it, the healthcheck names it, three documents name it, and the only thing on the other side is a step list this plan deletes.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: Only because CLAUDE.md asked for it to be settled here rather than assumed.

open_rulings.question: Three things are pushed out of these eight steps that a reader might expect in them: Caddy (and with it the limiter-behind-proxy leg), the `.env.example` / config.Load coverage leg, and the media sweep. The first two are one leg and one service; the third has a schedule of nobody.
open_rulings.recommendation: Accept. Eight steps is §1's bound and four of these eight are already large. All three are named in next_slice with their reasons, and the limiter deferral is stated as a live wrongness rather than as an absence.
open_rulings.why_it_needs_a_human: Because deferring the same thing twice is how it becomes permanent, and this is the second time Caddy has been deferred.

open_rulings.question: DEC-79 orders object storage and the media routes BEFORE `make seed`, which puts the plan's biggest evidence win — four lists that have never been read back from PostgreSQL — three steps out.
open_rulings.recommendation: Accept, and the argument is in DEC-79 with the two alternatives that were rejected and why. But it is the single most challengeable decision in this plan and it is flagged as such rather than buried.

execution.mode: One worker per step, sequential, with a review between steps. R5, R6 and R7 are mutually independent once R4 lands and may be reviewed in any order — but they are not parallel zones, because all three write to internal/httpapi/routes.go and internal/postgres, and `parallel_zones` requires disjoint sole-write paths (§3).
execution.test_first: MANDATORY, §6.7, and it is inherited from the client's own record rather than imposed: 'Test-first for new behaviour. When tests must come after — porting, integrating generated code — say so and name what gets backfilled.' Every behavioural step above carries its first failing test IN FULL and states what the red must say. A test that passes before the implementation exists is testing something else, and that is discovered now or never.
execution.write_it_and_break_it: §8, EVERY test and not only guards. A test that has never been red has never been shown to work, and a green suite cannot tell the difference. Under test-first this is nearly free — step 2 already ran it red — so the only deliberate breaks needed are for tests written against code that already works, and those are LABELLED backfill.
execution.restore_by_file_copy_never_git_checkout: The client's plans say it, this project's VS2 lost a step's implementation by ignoring it, and six of thirteen mutation results were contaminated. Against an uncommitted tree `git checkout --` no-ops on untracked files and restores tracked ones from the index, so mutations stack and a later red belongs to an earlier one — while the suite keeps going red, which looks exactly like success.
execution.a_mutation_that_did_not_change_the_file: proves nothing. Diff before running, and check the sha256 moved. One mutation in VS6 changed a comment inside a SQL string and left the suite green.
execution.note: Two things this plan asks for that are easy to skip and are the reason the last four steps are trustworthy or not. First, DEC-81: the arc grows in the same commit as the route, and the reviewer's first check is `git show --stat` against scripts/slice-arc.sh. Second, the INTERMEDIATE RED in R2 — a leg written after the correct implementation cannot demonstrate that it would have caught the defect, and R2's defect is one that looks correct for the whole of development.
